title: Orbit vs Orbital — 10-Point Delta Table & the s-Orbital
notes: **Orbit vs orbital (10-point delta):** (1) an orbit is a definite circular path; an orbital is a region of high probability. (2) Orbits are planar; orbitals are three-dimensional. (3) Orbits come from Bohr's model; orbitals from quantum mechanics. (4) An orbit has a fixed radius; an orbital has no sharp boundary. (5) Orbits are described by one quantum number (n); orbitals by three (n, l, m). (6) Orbits imply exact position and momentum; orbitals obey the uncertainty principle. (7) Orbits can hold at most 2n² electrons; orbitals hold at most 2 electrons. (8) Orbits are circular; orbitals have varied shapes (spherical, dumb-bell, etc.). (9) Orbits are not observable; orbitals are mapped by probability density ψ². (10) Orbits were abandoned; orbitals are the accepted modern description.

**Electronic arrays:** the electron configurations of representative atoms follow the Bohr–Bury order — N (Z=7): 1s² 2s² 2p³; O (Z=8): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴; Ne (Z=10): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Mg (Z=12): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²; Cl (Z=17): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵.

**s-orbital sharp metrics:** the s-orbital is spherical, non-directional, has no nodal plane, and its probability density is highest at the nucleus; it is the only orbital with a non-zero value at the nucleus.
**Opposite spins cancellation:** two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins (+½ and −½); their magnetic moments cancel, so a fully paired orbital contributes no net magnetism.
